source: The prevalence of malaria parasites in bloodfed mosquitoes identified via PCR of head and thorax was higher at the end versus start and peak of the transmission season (23.4, 4.9 and 8.0%, respectively), and slightly higher in singly-matched mosquitoes compared to mosquitoes with multiple meal sources (Table 2).
evidence: Direct statement with data on mosquito infection prevalence.

claim: Malaria parasite prevalence in bloodfed mosquitoes was slightly higher in singly-matched mosquitoes compared to mosquitoes with multiple meal sources.
source: The prevalence of malaria parasites in bloodfed mosquitoes identified via PCR of head and thorax was higher at the end versus start and peak of the transmission season (23.4, 4.9 and 8.0%, respectively), and slightly higher in singly-matched mosquitoes compared to mosquitoes with multiple meal sources (Table 2).
evidence: Direct statement comparing infection prevalence by blood meal type.

claim: A. coluzzii mosquitoes were less often infected compared to A. gambiae s.s. (odds ratio 0.41, 95% CI 0.22–0.76).
source: A. coluzzii mosquitoes were less often infected compared to A. gambiae s. s. (odds ratio 0.41 95% CI, 0.22–0.76 in a model that adjusted for timing of survey).
evidence: Direct statement with statistical analysis comparing infection rates between species.

claim: Only 7.7% of study subjects were linked to one or more potentially infectious mosquito meals at the start of the transmission season.
source: Only 7.7, 23.6% and 10.5% of study subjects were linked to one or more potentially infectious mosquito meals at the start, peak and end of transmission season, respectively.
evidence: Direct statement providing data on exposure to infected mosquitoes.

claim: Only 23.6% of study subjects were linked to one or more potentially infectious mosquito meals at the peak of the transmission season.
source: Only 7.7, 23.6% and 10.5% of study subjects were linked to one or more potentially infectious mosquito meals at the start, peak and end of transmission season, respectively.
evidence: Direct statement providing data on exposure to infected mosquitoes.

claim: Only 10.5% of study subjects were linked to one or more potentially infectious mosquito meals at the end of the transmission season.
source: Only 7.7, 23.6% and 10.5% of study subjects were linked to one or more potentially infectious mosquito meals at the start, peak and end of transmission season, respectively.
evidence: Direct statement providing data on exposure to infected mosquitoes.

claim: In each survey, the two individuals with the highest numbers of matched meals from infected mosquitoes experienced 44–50% of all exposure to infected mosquitoes.
source: In each survey, the two individuals with the highest numbers of matched meals from infected mosquitoes experienced 44–50% of all exposure to infected mosquitoes.
evidence: Direct statement showing extreme concentration of infectious bites.

claim: There was a positive association between the number of potentially infective mosquito bites an individual received and the total number of matched meals regardless of mosquito parasitological status (p<0.001).
source: As expected, there was a positive association between the number of potentially infective mosquito bites an individual received and the total number of matched meals regardless of mosquito parasitological status (Figure 3b, p<0.001 in a mixed effects negative binomial model that had the total number of matched blood meals as a covariate and only included individuals with at least one matched meal).
evidence: Direct statement with statistical analysis showing positive association.

claim: There was evidence of household-level clustering of infectious bites (intra-class correlation 0.19, 95% CI 0.08–0.38, p<0.001).
source: Conditional on the total number of bites, there was evidence of household-level clustering of infectious bites (intra-class [household] correlation 0.19, 95% CI 0.08–0.38, p<0.001 in a mixed effects logistic model that included singly matched mosquitoes); however, there was no evidence of individual-level clustering after adjustment for household-related variability (p=0.50).
evidence: Direct statement with statistical analysis showing household clustering.

claim: There was no evidence of individual-level clustering of infectious bites after adjustment for household-related variability (p=0.50).
source: Conditional on the total number of bites, there was evidence of household-level clustering of infectious bites (intra-class [household] correlation 0.19, 95% CI 0.08–0.38, p<0.001 in a mixed effects logistic model that included singly matched mosquitoes); however, there was no evidence of individual-level clustering after adjustment for household-related variability (p=0.50).
evidence: Direct statement with statistical analysis showing no individual clustering.

claim: The observed degree of mosquito biting heterogeneity could be linked to a 3-fold or higher increase in malaria R0 compared to a random-mixing system.
source: Applying simple, well-established (Smith et al., 2007; Churcher et al., 2015) methods, we estimated that the observed degree of mosquito biting heterogeneity could be linked to a 3-fold or higher increase in malaria R0 compared to a random-mixing system.
evidence: Direct statement with citation to established methods and estimate of R0 increase.

claim: R0 is increased by a factor of 4.8 in settings where mosquito exposure and its variability are similar to those observed at the start of the transmission season.
source: Figure 4 illustrates the impact that more extreme heterogeneity can have on the calculated R0 of malaria: R0 is increased by a factor of 4.8, 4.2 and 8.4 in settings where mosquito exposure and its variability are similar to those observed at the start, peak and end of the transmission season in our study area.
evidence: Direct statement with reference to figure showing R0 calculations.

claim: R0 is increased by a factor of 4.2 in settings where mosquito exposure and its variability are similar to those observed at the peak of the transmission season.
source: Figure 4 illustrates the impact that more extreme heterogeneity can have on the calculated R0 of malaria: R0 is increased by a factor of 4.8, 4.2 and 8.4 in settings where mosquito exposure and its variability are similar to those observed at the start, peak and end of the transmission season in our study area.
evidence: Direct statement with reference to figure showing R0 calculations.

claim: R0 is increased by a factor of 8.4 in settings where mosquito exposure and its variability are similar to those observed at the end of the transmission season.
source: Figure 4 illustrates the impact that more extreme heterogeneity can have on the calculated R0 of malaria: R0 is increased by a factor of 4.8, 4.2 and 8.4 in settings where mosquito exposure and its variability are similar to those observed at the start, peak and end of the transmission season in our study area.
evidence: Direct statement with reference to figure showing R0 calculations.

claim: In sensitivity analysis that allocates multiply fed mosquitoes' meals to the least exposed individuals, R0 increases by a factor of 3.3 at the start of the transmission season.
source: R0 is high even when the skew is reduced by the conservative sensitivity analysis that allocates multiply fed mosquitoes' meals to the least exposed individuals, yielding R0 increases by a factor of 3.3, 3.2 and 5.7 at the start, peak and end of the transmission season, respectively.
evidence: Direct statement providing sensitivity analysis results.

claim: In sensitivity analysis that allocates multiply fed mosquitoes' meals to the least exposed individuals, R0 increases by a factor of 3.2 at the peak of the transmission season.
source: R0 is high even when the skew is reduced by the conservative sensitivity analysis that allocates multiply fed mosquitoes' meals to the least exposed individuals, yielding R0 increases by a factor of 3.3, 3.2 and 5.7 at the start, peak and end of the transmission season, respectively.
evidence: Direct statement providing sensitivity analysis results.

claim: In sensitivity analysis that allocates multiply fed mosquitoes' meals to the least exposed individuals, R0 increases by a factor of 5.7 at the end of the transmission season.
source: R0 is high even when the skew is reduced by the conservative sensitivity analysis that allocates multiply fed mosquitoes' meals to the least exposed individuals, yielding R0 increases by a factor of 3.3, 3.2 and 5.7 at the start, peak and end of the transmission season, respectively.
evidence: Direct statement providing sensitivity analysis results.

claim: The distribution of mosquito bites exceeded the Pareto rule (20/80) in two of the three surveys performed (20/85 and 20/96).
source: We observed that the distribution of mosquito bites exceeded the Pareto rule (20/80) in two of the three surveys performed (20/85, 76, and 96) and, at its most pronounced, is estimated to have profound epidemiological consequences, inflating the basic reproduction number of malaria by 8-fold.
evidence: Direct statement in the abstract summarizing the findings.

claim: At its most pronounced, heterogeneity in mosquito biting is estimated to inflate the basic reproduction number of malaria by 8-fold.
source: We observed that the distribution of mosquito bites exceeded the Pareto rule (20/80) in two of the three surveys performed (20/85, 76, and 96) and, at its most pronounced, is estimated to have profound epidemiological consequences, inflating the basic reproduction number of malaria by 8-fold.
evidence: Direct statement in the abstract summarizing the R0 calculation.

claim: The distribution of bites from sporozoite-positive mosquitoes followed a similar pattern to overall bites, with a small number of individuals within households receiving multiple potentially infectious bites over the period of a few days.
source: The distribution of bites from sporozoite-positive mosquitoes followed a similar pattern, with a small number of individuals within households receiving multiple potentially infectious bites over the period of a few days.
evidence: Direct statement in the abstract describing the distribution of infectious bites.

claim: Heterogeneity in mosquito exposure contributes considerably to heterogeneity in infection risk.
source: Together, our findings indicate that heterogeneity in mosquito exposure contributes considerably to heterogeneity in infection risk and suggest significant variation in malaria transmission potential.
evidence: Direct conclusion stated in the abstract.

claim: There is significant variation in malaria transmission potential.
source: Together, our findings indicate that heterogeneity in mosquito exposure contributes considerably to heterogeneity in infection risk and suggest significant variation in malaria transmission potential.
evidence: Direct conclusion stated in the abstract.

claim: Malaria epidemiology is doubly dependent on the frequency and efficiency of contacts between human hosts and Anopheles mosquitoes.
source: Malaria epidemiology is doubly dependent on the frequency and efficiency of contacts between human hosts and Anopheles mosquitoes, which link the number of mosquito infections caused by an infectious human host and the rate at which uninfected humans acquire infections.
evidence: Direct statement in the introduction establishing the importance of human-mosquito contact.

claim: Even within the same locality individuals may not be equally likely to be bitten by Anopheles mosquitoes.
source: While at a local level vector density determines average mosquito exposure, even within the same locality individuals may not be equally likely to be bitten by Anopheles mosquitoes (Lindsay et al., 1993; Knols et al., 1995a; Carnevale et al., 1978; Muirhead-Thomson, 1951).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Exposure to malaria vectors is influenced by host availability and attractiveness to mosquitoes.
source: Exposure to malaria vectors is influenced by host availability (i.e., amount of time an individual remains unprotected against mosquito bites in an environment where anopheline mosquitoes are present) and attractiveness to mosquitoes (Stone et al., 2015; Yakob, 2016).
evidence: Direct statement with citations supporting the factors influencing exposure.

claim: More than three quarters of human exposure to anopheline mosquito bites occur when individuals are indoors.
source: Availability determines when and where individuals might be sampled by mosquitoes: a multicentre study in Africa that collected entomological and human behavioural data estimated that more than three quarters of human exposure to anopheline mosquito bites occur when individuals are indoors (Huho et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to a multicentre study.

claim: Age and body surface area are two major determinants of attractiveness to mosquitoes.
source: For individuals who are accessible to malaria vectors, age and body surface area (Carnevale et al., 1978; Port et al., 1980) are two major determinants of attractiveness to mosquitoes, although other factors also play a role (Knols et al., 1995a).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Previously the authors have shown that mosquitoes in this study area fed more often on adults.
source: Previously we have shown that these mosquitoes fed more often on adults (Gonçalves et al., 2017).
evidence: Reference to previous publication by the same authors.

claim: At the peak of the transmission season, the household with the highest number of fed mosquitoes had ~150 times more than the household with the lowest number.
source: Indeed, at the peak of the transmission season, the household with the highest number of fed mosquitoes had ~150 times more than the household with the lowest number.
evidence: Direct statement describing between-household variation.

claim: Household characteristics such as construction material, number of windows, eaves as well as geographical proximity to mosquito breeding sites have been previously associated with increased exposure to mosquitoes indoors.
source: Household characteristics such as construction material, number of windows, eaves as well as geographical proximity to mosquito breeding sites have all been previously associated with increased exposure to mosquitoes indoors and explain some of the between-household variation in mosquito abundance.
evidence: Statement about factors known from previous research to affect mosquito exposure.

claim: A study in Kenya showed that foci of clinical malaria are unstable and that one-month surveillance data might only have predictive value of higher-than-average transmission over short periods of time.
source: A study in Kenya (Bejon et al., 2014) showed that foci of clinical malaria are unstable and that one-month surveillance data, for example, might only have predictive value of higher-than-average transmission over short periods of time.
evidence: Statement supported by citation to a study in Kenya.

claim: The ranking of households according to the number of infected mosquito bites per individual varies over time.
source: This is consistent with our observation that the ranking of households according to the number of infected mosquito bites per individual varies over time (Figure 3) and poses considerable challenges to sustainably targeting high exposure households for maximum community benefit.
evidence: Direct statement with reference to figure showing temporal variation.

claim: At the peak of the transmission season, the maximum difference in numbers of matched meals for participants in the same house ranged from 1 to 51.
source: At the peak of the transmission season, the maximum difference in numbers of matched meals for participants in the same house ranged from 1 to 51, that is a difference of up to ~10 mosquito bites per day.
evidence: Direct statement describing within-household variation in exposure.

claim: Blood meals from 8.2% of tested mosquitoes did not amplify for human DNA.
source: Furthermore, we observed that blood meals from 8.2% of tested mosquitoes did not amplify for human DNA.
evidence: Direct statement providing data on failed amplifications.

claim: Analyses only used data from ~70% of all successfully typed mosquito meals.
source: A technical limitation of this study was that our analyses only used data from ~70% of all successfully typed mosquito meals.
evidence: Direct statement acknowledging a limitation of the analysis.

claim: 139/292 unmatched mosquito meals were single blood meals from individuals not in the study houses.
source: Of those not matched, 139/292 were single blood meals from individuals not in our study houses and 153/292 had evidence of multiple blood meals.
evidence: Direct statement providing data on unmatched blood meals.

claim: 153/292 unmatched mosquito meals had evidence of multiple blood meals.
source: Of those not matched, 139/292 were single blood meals from individuals not in our study houses and 153/292 had evidence of multiple blood meals.
evidence: Direct statement providing data on multiple-source blood meals.

claim: The genetic profiles of unmatched blood meals suggest a heterogeneous feeding pattern.
source: The genetic profiles of these unmatched blood meals also suggest a heterogeneous feeding pattern: in the three houses with more than 10 unmatched mosquitoes, 16/41, 8/13 and 31/33 blood meals had the same profile.
evidence: Direct statement with data supporting heterogeneous feeding pattern.

claim: Broad differences in anthropophily between mosquito species are well recognised.
source: Broad differences in anthropophily between mosquito species are well recognised (Takken and Verhulst, 2013) however there are fewer data (Knols et al., 1995b) on whether different Anopheles species have different feeding preferences with regards to individual humans.
evidence: Statement supported by citation to previous research.

claim: There are fewer data on whether different Anopheles species have different feeding preferences with regards to individual humans.
source: Broad differences in anthropophily between mosquito species are well recognised (Takken and Verhulst, 2013) however there are fewer data (Knols et al., 1995b) on whether different Anopheles species have different feeding preferences with regards to individual humans.
evidence: Statement supported by citation indicating limited research on this topic.

claim: Exposure to one mosquito species was positively associated with exposure to the others.
source: Although seasonal differences in species abundance were evident, we observed aggregation in human biting irrespective of vector species and exposure to one species was positively associated with exposure to the others.
evidence: Direct statement describing the relationship between exposures to different species.

claim: There is evidence from membrane feeding experiments performed in Senegal that A. gambiae s.s. mosquitoes might be more susceptible to malaria infection.
source: There is evidence from membrane feeding experiments performed in Senegal (Ndiath et al., 2011) that A. gambiae s. s. mosquitoes might be more susceptible to malaria infection, although this association was not observed in another transmission study (Gnémé et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to experimental study, with caveat about conflicting evidence.

claim: The higher frequency of falciparum infection in A. gambiae s.s. mosquitoes confirms the prime importance of this species for malaria transmission in the study setting.
source: The higher frequency of falciparum infection in A. gambiae s. s. mosquitoes confirms, together with its relatively high abundance, the prime importance of this species for malaria transmission in the study setting.
evidence: Inference drawn from the infection data and species abundance.

claim: Mosquitoes with multiple blood meals are more likely to infect more than one individual on a single night compared to mosquitoes with single-source blood meals.
source: The contributions of the different Anopheles species to the mosquito infectious reservoir also depend on the number of potential parasite inoculations per mosquito-time: mosquitoes with multiple blood meals are more likely to infect more than one individual on a single night compared to mosquitoes with single-source blood meals, assuming sufficient quantities of sporozoites are inoculated during the probing of the different hosts.
evidence: Logical inference about the transmission potential of mosquitoes with multiple blood meals.

claim: Species composition of local vector populations varies in the course of the rainy season.
source: Importantly, as species composition of local vector populations varies in the course of the rainy season (Dao et al., 2014), these differences might impact the rate of infection propagation in human populations over the course of a single transmission season as relative abundances of the different vector species change.
evidence: Statement supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Between 75% and 90% of the study participants were not matched to feeding by infected mosquitoes during the three study periods.
source: At the individual level, a few individuals received multiple potentially infective bites while between 75% and 90% of the study participants were not matched to feeding by infected mosquitoes during the three study periods.
evidence: Direct statement providing data on exposure to infected mosquitoes.

claim: The use of blood meal genotyping with concurrent assessment of mosquito sporozoite carriage during epidemiological studies could improve our understanding of the heterogeneity in clinical malaria risk.
source: These results also suggest that the use of blood meal genotyping with concurrent assessment of mosquito sporozoite carriage during epidemiological studies could improve our understanding of the heterogeneity in clinical malaria risk (Mwangi et al., 2008; Loucoubar et al., 2013; Ndungu et al., 2015).
evidence: Suggestion for future research supported by citations to relevant studies.

claim: Clustering of sporozoite-positive mosquito bites at the household level was not related to local mosquito abundance.
source: Furthermore, whilst we observed a positive association between the total number of mosquito bites and the number of bites from sporozoite infected mosquitoes at the individual level, our data suggest clustering of sporozoite-positive mosquito bites at the household level that was not related to local mosquito abundance.
evidence: Direct statement describing the pattern of infectious bite clustering.

claim: Household-level clustering of infectious bites could be linked to a correlation between prevalence of infection in mosquitoes and in humans in the same households assuming limited mixing.
source: This phenomenon could be linked to (i) a correlation between prevalence of infection in mosquitoes and in humans in the same households assuming limited mixing of mosquitoes and humans (e.g. due to the presence of breeding sites near houses, reducing the distances travelled by mosquitoes between consecutive blood meals [Le Menach et al., 2005], or to feeding site-fidelity in Anopheles mosquitoes [McCall et al., 2001]) or possibly to (ii) factors which affect mosquito survival on a very local scale, since mosquito age is associated with cumulative risk of sporozoite infection (Lines et al., 1991).
evidence: Speculative explanation supported by citations to relevant studies.

claim: Mosquito age is associated with cumulative risk of sporozoite infection.
source: This phenomenon could be linked to (i) a correlation between prevalence of infection in mosquitoes and in humans in the same households assuming limited mixing of mosquitoes and humans (e.g. due to the presence of breeding sites near houses, reducing the distances travelled by mosquitoes between consecutive blood meals [Le Menach et al., 2005], or to feeding site-fidelity in Anopheles mosquitoes [McCall et al., 2001]) or possibly to (ii) factors which affect mosquito survival on a very local scale, since mosquito age is associated with cumulative risk of sporozoite infection (Lines et al., 1991).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Only limited data are available for natural exposure to Anopheles mosquitoes.
source: In summary, although studies have assessed natural exposure to vectors of other infections, such as Aedes (Harrington et al., 2014; Liebman et al., 2014) and Culex (Michael et al., 2001), only limited data are available for Anopheles mosquitoes (Soremekun et al., 2004; Scott et al., 2006).
evidence: Statement supported by citations indicating limited previous research.

claim: The findings support the design of interventions that aim to reduce transmission by targeting a small proportion of the population.
source: In our field site, characterized by high malaria transmission intensity, we show significant heterogeneity both between and within households in terms of the number of mosquito blood meals and the distribution of potentially infectious mosquito feedings; these patterns are consistent with the 20/80 rule and support the design of interventions that aim to reduce transmission by targeting a small proportion of the population.
evidence: Inference drawn from the heterogeneity findings about intervention design.

claim: Opportunities to specifically target high-exposure households depend on the operational feasibility to identify these households and the stability in exposure over time.
source: Opportunities to specifically target high-exposure households depend on the operational feasibility to identify these households and the stability in exposure over time.
evidence: Statement about practical considerations for targeted interventions.

claim: Ethical clearance was obtained from the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine ethics committee (reference number 6447).
source: Ethical clearance was obtained from the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine ethics committee (reference number 6447), and the ethical review committee of the Ministry of Health of Burkina Faso (2013-7-58).
evidence: Direct statement about ethical approval.

claim: Ethical clearance was obtained from the ethical review committee of the Ministry of Health of Burkina Faso (2013-7-58).
source: Ethical clearance was obtained from the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine ethics committee (reference number 6447), and the ethical review committee of the Ministry of Health of Burkina Faso (2013-7-58).
evidence: Direct statement about ethical approval.
